AK: The incoming identity was unresolved at the November 4 cutoff. Keep the researched candidates separate; do not assign the leading candidate's position to an elected governor.
AL: Tuberville welcomes locally accepted projects, rejects a blanket moratorium, and proposes ending incentives and making developers pay infrastructure and resource costs. These are campaign proposals. His earlier federal procedural vote is not a gubernatorial action.
AR: Sanders endorses Google and AVAIO investment and praises incentives and faster approvals, while calling for project-specific scrutiny of utility costs, water and benefits. Announcements and company promises do not establish completed projects or protected bills.
AZ: Hobbs rejects a statewide construction moratorium and favors suitable, resource-conscious projects paying their costs. The enacted 2026–29 pause covers new tax qualifications, not construction; her broader repeal and water-charge positions must remain separate from enacted law.
CA: Becerra expresses openness if projects provide community jobs and additional energy while protecting water. A firsthand advocacy account attributes rejection of a moratorium to him, but its event date and recording were not verified. No implemented gubernatorial policy is established.
CO: Weiser rejects a construction moratorium, favors local choice and developer-paid costs, clean power and water safeguards, and is open to targeted incentives in transition communities. His promised first-priority legislation is a proposal, not enacted law.
CT: Opposes hyperscale growth; retains narrower exceptions

Lamont opposes large AI/hyperscale centers and says new demand should bring generation, while allowing enterprise IT upgrades and possible self-supplied, locally accepted projects. His 2021 incentive support is contrary history; claimed past rejections were not matched to actual denial instruments.
DE: Conditional development with signed cost/disclosure laws

Meyer welcomes responsible development but rejects household cost shifts and grid threats. He signed large-load cost/security, incentive and NDA restrictions. Their thresholds and clean-energy exceptions matter; the PSC interconnection pause is not a gubernatorial statewide construction ban.
FL: Donalds supports domestic development with slower, safeguarded expansion rather than a statewide moratorium, local ability to refuse, and developer-paid resource costs. His federal bill and House vote are not gubernatorial enactments, and asserted bill guarantees exceed the verified statutory scope.
GA: Bottoms seeks a pause on new construction, cost and resource safeguards, transparency and community protections. November 4 reporting attributes a planned executive order and tax-agreement review to her; implementation and legal sufficiency remain unresolved. Her defense of a smaller Georgia Tech project qualifies blanket-opposition readings.
HI: Green's verified evidence concerns state IT resilience and a project-specific public data-center relocation budget reduction. It does not establish support for or opposition to statewide private hyperscale construction. Do not turn this evidence gap into a neutral stance.
IA: Conditional development; proposes ending tax breaks

Sand welcomes projects contributing locally, with developer-paid utility and infrastructure costs, monitoring, transparency and enforceable accountability. He proposes ending data-center tax breaks. These are prospective safeguards and repeal proposals, not implemented tariffs or guaranteed savings.
ID: Little promotes investment and coordinated faster review, while supporting developer responsibility for incremental power costs and community voice. His cost-protection law, executive review council and voluntary pledge are distinct instruments; the pledge itself is not a binding local veto or tariff.
IL: Pritzker paused new incentive processing while honoring prior agreements; this is not a construction ban. He proposes stronger utility-cost, generation, water and community safeguards. The directive's authority is disputed, and proposed protections should not be reported as enacted tariffs.
IN: Active development promotion; local and cost conditions

Braun defends aggressive development and endorses major investment, while supporting community suitability, developer power supply and local benefits. His later objection to local abatements does not repeal state sales-tax exemptions or erase earlier incentive commitments.
KS: The incoming identity was unresolved at the cutoff. Holscher and Masterson have separate researched comparisons, including different pause and incentive positions; neither is substituted for a verified winner, and Laura Kelly is predecessor evidence only.
KY: Conditional development under announced executive safeguards

Beshear's official announcement describes an executive order protecting utility customers, resources and local choice. The standalone order was inaccessible, so the verified scope is the announcement, not independently inspected operative text or proven enforcement. No statewide ban or achieved bill protection is established.
LA: Development and incentives with executive conditions

Landry promotes Meta and other development alongside tax incentives. His executive order conditions incentive participation on cost responsibility, resources and community benefits. Existing-contract treatment remains unresolved; the historical confidentiality agreement is retained as contrary transparency evidence.
MA: Healey supports development subject to community, clean-energy, water and ratepayer protections and suspended new exemption applications. The signed permitting order remained inaccessible, so its scope is attributed to original reporting. Neither a construction ban nor a universal municipal veto is established.
MD: Executive alignment framework; proposes tax repeal

Moore's signed order offers coordinated review to aligned projects under cost, resource, disclosure and local-approval criteria. It is not a construction moratorium. He proposes repealing the sales/use exemption; earlier backup-generator streamlining and a study veto remain visible as contrary history.
ME: Pingree proposes an AI-data-center moratorium until strong ratepayer, water, environmental and community protections exist, while allowing future compliant development. Her willingness to sign the earlier vetoed limitation is advocacy, not a law she enacted or a permanent blanket ban.
MI: Benson calls for a moratorium until enforceable water, energy-cost and community safeguards exist, with transparent negotiations and union jobs. Earlier conditional openness and stricter water wording remain visible. Broad tax-break opposition and a later narrower formulation are both proposals, not enacted repeal.
MN: Local choice and stronger review; resists statewide pause

Klobuchar emphasizes local decisions, negotiation disclosure, environmental safeguards and no household cost shifts. Reporting attributes resistance to a statewide pause in favor of stronger review. Her federal procedural vote is distinct from future gubernatorial action, and no numeric water cap is established.
MO: Development promotion with review and cost protections

Kehoe promotes major investments while conditioning suitable projects on energy affordability, water and local support. His review order is not a construction pause; signed large-load tariff provisions and proposed next-session guardrails remain distinct from project announcements and voluntary pledges.
MS: Reeves promotes AWS and xAI investment, public assistance and enabling legislation, and opposes local and national pauses. His support for continued xAI turbine power and assurances about household costs are retained, without treating prospective investment or claimed savings as verified outcomes.
MT: Gianforte promotes investment, permitting coordination and onsite supply while advocating developer-paid incremental costs, agricultural water protection and community engagement. Signed computation and generation laws are distinct from prospective projects; utility contract safeguards still depend on independent PSC review.
NC: Development support; pushes cost and clean-power rules

Stein endorses Amazon investment and calls for developers to bear full costs and provide clean power. His energy task force and tariff advocacy are not themselves final commission tariffs or construction approvals; proposed protections and projected bill effects remain unproven outcomes.
ND: Armstrong praises Applied Digital expansion and sees opportunities where communities want investment, while rejecting consumer cost shifts. His backup-generation siting exemption is narrow and does not exempt the whole campus from local or environmental approvals. Expected jobs and capacity are not completed outcomes.
NE: Incentive restriction; rejects blanket construction ban

Pillen announces an end to new incentive approvals and orders resource review, while later rejecting a complete ban and favoring case-specific local decisions, developer costs and additional taxation. The operative order's review language and narrower enacted self-generation rules qualify broader rhetoric.
NH: Advocates statewide moratorium; not yet enacted

Ayotte supports a multi-year statewide pause through a future budget and opposes Bow and Nottingham projects on power and resource grounds. No executed statewide ban is established. Her earlier off-grid utility-regulation exemption remains contrary enabling history, not proof that every project is exempt.
NJ: Conditional development with signed utility/reporting laws

Sherrill supports guarded development, signed large-load cost and flexibility legislation and water/energy reporting requirements, and supports a specific shared-computing initiative in existing facilities. Threshold-setting, implementation deadlines, confidentiality and exemptions qualify broader claims of immediate universal obligations.
NM: Proposed pause on new large-scale construction

Haaland proposes a temporary pause until statewide safeguards exist, including clean power, cooling, labor and community protections. Her campaign excludes projects already underway from the construction pause; future regulation of existing facilities remains unresolved. This is not an order already issued as governor.
NV: Proposed tax-abatement pause; construction ban not established

Ford proposes pausing new abatements pending benefit audits, plus developer-paid costs, clean energy and restrictions on evaporative cooling. These are prospective accountability policies, not an enacted construction moratorium, permanent incentive abolition or verified resource outcomes.
NY: Hochul's EO62 holds incomplete covered DEC discretionary applications pending the final GEIS report and findings; local approvals remain unaffected. Its 50MW site scope and institutional exemptions matter. Support for exempt Empire AI research computing does not negate the narrower hold or imply opposition to all facilities.
OH: Acton proposes pausing new construction until cost, generation, labor, transparency and resource safeguards exist. Incentive restraint is not verified categorical sales-tax repeal; the legal vehicle, thresholds and grandfathering remain unknown. A separate wastewater-well moratorium is not a data-center action.
OK: Mazzei welcomes locally approved industrial-site projects that pay their own electricity, water and infrastructure costs without special tax breaks or taxpayer funding. Closed-loop cooling claims are proposed preferences, not verified water performance; no implemented tariff or repeal is established.
OR: Scoped state-land/permit pauses; broader pause advocacy

Kotek terminated a specific state-land sale, paused specified state-property actions, requested a discretionary environmental-permit pause and supports local moratoria. These scoped measures are not a universal private-land construction ban. Her broader pause and 2027 legislative commitments remain prospective, alongside earlier incentive support.
PA: Stronger permitting conditions after earlier promotion

Shapiro promoted Amazon and Fast Track review, then removed data centers from Fast Track and imposed different GRID agreement/non-signer pathways. He advocates guardrails rather than a general moratorium. The order retains a non-signer route; neither prospective agreements nor tariff petitions prove delivered protections or canceled projects.
RI: Foulkes assented to a statewide data-center ban in an August interview transcript, after earlier openness to a moratorium, and opposed a proposed equipment tax exemption. Duration, threshold, exemptions, existing-site treatment and legal route remain unspecified; no enacted ban or inspected audiovisual delivery is established.
SC: Wilson supports willing-community development, local refusal and developer-paid costs, own supply and statewide safeguards. Stronger own-energy language and later incentive-based self-generation language coexist. Neither a final tariff nor every clause of another legislator's bill is established as his policy.
SD: Rhoden signed cost-allocation and water safeguards and a nonpreemption provision preserving local restrictions, including local prohibitions. This is not a statewide moratorium. His earlier incentive openness and later qualifications remain visible rather than being collapsed into blanket subsidy opposition.
TN: Conditional growth; local refusal and supply expansion

Blackburn supports responsible growth in willing communities, local refusal, ratepayer legislation and environmental/noise safeguards, while opposing a particular Nashville Zoo-adjacent location. Her TVA nuclear advocacy and federal-role actions do not establish licensed generation or gubernatorial project approval.
TX: Hinojosa calls for a pause until protective laws, with stronger local powers, developer-paid costs, water protection, labor conditions, transparency and subsidy opposition. Earlier incentive votes and her SB6 Yea remain contrary or qualifying history; the HB3104 final recorded Yea also carries her stated intended No. No gubernatorial moratorium is enacted by her campaign pledge.
UT: Cox supports suitable projects and faster development while directing covered agencies to protect resources and provide public comment. His order does not bind every independent/local entity or create a statewide ban. Earlier caution about low-job resource-intensive projects and later promotion are both retained; signed large-load cost provisions are separate from achieved bill outcomes.
VA: Continued investment with stronger executive/legislative rules

Spanberger supports continued investment with community, environmental and cost obligations. Her order restricts specified NDAs and removes new 25MW-plus projects from certain assistance; ordinary permits are not banned. Signed sound/emissions/tax measures and proposed 2027 requirements have different scopes and should not be conflated.
VT: Mixed chronology: vetoed package; later pause support attributed

Scott vetoed H727 as unnecessary/economically harmful, accepts local moratoria and says Vermont need not depend on data centers. A later campaign-spokesman statement supports a large-center construction moratorium pending federal action. Preserve this newer qualification without treating it as an enacted order or direct personal quotation.
WA: Ferguson commissioned impact study, signed targeted removal of refurbishment/replacement exemptions while retaining qualifying new-construction eligibility, and extended specified clean-energy coverage. These are not repeal of every incentive, a universal onsite-generation mandate or a construction ban.
WI: Later conditional statewide pause and tax-repeal support

Crowley supports local authority, developer-paid costs, clean energy and community benefits. Later interviews support a statewide pause during environmental review and tax-exemption repeal, qualifying earlier skepticism about a future-only moratorium. Conflicting debate terminology remains visible; no enacted statewide pause is established.
WV: Strong development facilitation; specified local preemption

Morrisey promotes certified high-impact data centers and microgrids under signed legislation preempting specified local controls. Cost-protection provisions and later advisory/resource promises do not restore a municipal veto or establish achieved savings or universal water limits. Certification and investment announcements are not construction completion.
WY: Conditional development; rejects outright permitting moratorium

Barlow supports locally suitable projects with water protection, company-paid energy costs and better information, and opposes an outright permitting moratorium. He remains open to coal and gas supply. His state-senate votes concern a transmission study and an unsuccessful tax-revenue proposal, not gubernatorial permits or enacted new rates.
